title: The Tur's four rows
hookLine: Jacob ben Asher arranges law in four "rows", the model for later codes
carry: a whole life fits in four rows
tomorrow: The table and the tablecloth today

lines: A BOOK OF LAW BORROWS THE PICTURE.
cards: Gold settings, and in them, stones. The book of Exodus describes a breastplate for the high priest, a square of woven cloth set with precious stones in four rows, each stone engraved with the name of a tribe.
The Torah lingers over it, stone by stone. Much later, a rabbi named Jacob ben Asher, a son of the Rosh you met two days ago, borrowed that picture for a book of law.
He called it the Four Rows, and people came to call it by one short word.

teach.b: Tur. A row. The full name is Arba'ah Turim, the Four Rows, and each row takes its name from a phrase in scripture.
The first row is Orach Chayim, the path of life: waking up, blessings, prayer, Shabbat, the festivals.
The second is Yoreh De'ah, he will teach knowledge: questions people often bring to a rabbi, what may be eaten, how to mourn, how to give charity, how to study Torah.

The third is Even HaEzer, the stone of help, named for the stone the prophet Samuel set up: marriage, divorce and family. The fourth is Choshen Mishpat, the breastplate of judgment: money, property, damages, the courts.
There the image comes full circle: the last row is named for the breastplate the whole book is built on. Now notice what's missing. Maimonides set out the laws of the Temple and of kings.

teach.h: THE LAW YOU COULD LIVE WHERE YOU WERE.
teach.b: Jacob ben Asher left those aside and arranged the law that people could live by where they were. Notice, too, how he writes.

Where Maimonides' code speaks in one voice, the Tur often names earlier authorities and lays their views side by side, and often gives his father's view. It's a code that still lets you hear a little of the conversation.
And the shape lasted: tomorrow's book keeps the very same four rows.

teach.h: A WHOLE LIFE IN FOUR ROWS.
teach.b: Prayer, food, family, money, and a whole life fits inside them.

how: The Tur is studied in yeshivas and by students of Jewish law, often alongside the Beit Yosef, a commentary printed with it. Its four section names are still used to organize Jewish law.

s: the Tur's name comes from a picture in Exodus
the high priest's breastplate held its stones in four rows.
the Tur sets out the laws of the Temple service
Jacob ben Asher left those aside and arranged the law people could live by where they were.
Choshen Mishpat is the row about prayer
it covers money, property, damages and courts; prayer is in Orach Chayim.

games.q: you're Jacob ben Asher, writing a code of law after Maimonides. what do you do with the laws that can't be kept without the Temple?
o: include every one of them, in full.
leave them aside and arrange the law people can live.
games.why: he leaves them aside and builds four rows of living law: prayer, food, family, money. later codes keep his shape.

practice: Walk through your day so far, and the part still ahead, and set each piece in a row: prayer or rest, what you eat and learn, the people you love, and work and what you owe others.
Don't judge any row; just notice which one is crowded and which is nearly empty.

wordCard.voice: Tur. A row. The short name for Jacob ben Asher's code of Jewish law, the Four Rows, arranged like the stones on the high priest's breastplate. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a row, as in the rows of stones on the high priest's breastplate.
